title: Largest number from a list of integers (custom comparator: compare `a+b` vs `b+a`).
shortTitle: Largest Number From a List of Integers — Custom Comparator a+b vs b+a

s1_definition.profdef: The Largest Number problem arranges a list of non-negative integers so their concatenation forms the biggest possible number. The correct ordering is defined by a custom comparator that, for any two numbers a and b, compares the concatenation of a-then-b against b-then-a as strings, placing first whichever yields the larger concatenation. After sorting with this comparator, you join the numbers, handling the all-zeros case. It runs in n-log-n time for the sort over the numbers.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to stitch a set of branch codes together into the single largest possible identifier for a priority label. The surprising part is you cannot just sort the numbers normally, because `9` should come before `30` even though `9` is smaller, since `930` beats `309`. The rule is: for any two codes, try gluing them both ways and keep the order that produces the bigger glued string. Sorting everything by that rule and joining gives the largest identifier.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sort by comparing the string a+b against b+a and put the bigger concatenation first.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Largest Number problem arranges a list of non-negative integers so their concatenation forms the biggest possible number. The correct ordering is defined by a custom comparator that, for any two numbers a and b, compares the concatenation of a-then-b against b-then-a as strings, placing first whichever yields the larger concatenation. After sorting with this comparator, you join the numbers, handling the all-zeros case. It runs in n-log-n time for the sort over the numbers.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to stitch a set of branch codes together into the single largest possible identifier for a priority label. The surprising part is you cannot just sort the numbers normally, because `9` should come before `30` even though `9` is smaller, since `930` beats `309`. The rule is: for any two codes, try gluing them both ways and keep the order that produces the bigger glued string. Sorting everything by that rule and joining gives the largest identifier.

**One line to remember:** Sort by comparing the string a+b against b+a and put the bigger concatenation first.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive instinct is to sort the numbers in descending order and concatenate, but that is wrong. Consider `3` and `30`. Descending order would place `30` before `3`, giving `303`, but `3` before `30` gives `330`, which is larger. Numeric size is the wrong key. What matters is which arrangement produces the larger concatenated string.

The correct comparator works on string concatenations. For two numbers a and b, you form the string a-followed-by-b and the string b-followed-by-a, both of which have the same length, and you compare them as strings. If a-then-b is larger, a should come first; if b-then-a is larger, b should come first. Because both concatenations have identical length, comparing them lexicographically as strings is the same as comparing them as numbers, so you avoid any overflow from building giant numeric values.

You convert all numbers to strings, sort the list with this comparator in descending concatenation order, and then join them in that sorted order. This greedy ordering is provably optimal: the comparator defines a total order, and any adjacent pair out of this order could be swapped to produce a strictly larger result, so the fully sorted arrangement is the maximum.

A senior point is why the comparator is a valid total order, which is what makes the sort correct. The relation defined by comparing a+b to b+a is transitive, which is not obvious but is a known property for this concatenation comparison on numeric strings. Because it is a consistent total order, a standard comparison sort produces the globally optimal arrangement, not just locally good swaps. Interviewers appreciate when you note that the greedy exchange argument relies on this transitivity.

Another senior point is the all-zeros edge case. If the input is several zeros, sorting and joining yields a string like `000`, but the largest number is just `0`. So after joining, if the first character is a zero, the entire result must be zero, which you return as the single string `0`. Forgetting this produces an invalid leading-zero result.

A small finance-domain example: `codes.sort((x, y) -> (y + x).compareTo(x + y));` sorts branch-code strings so their concatenation is largest, and `String.join("", codes)` builds the identifier, with the zero guard applied at the end.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India assembles a set of numeric branch codes into the single largest possible concatenated identifier used as a priority sort key for batch processing, so higher identifiers are processed first. Sorting the codes numerically gives the wrong identifier. Building the largest number by custom comparator is exactly this.

This is exactly how the Largest Number problem works in Java — a comparator that, for each pair, keeps the order whose concatenation is bigger.

Problem 2 — Sometimes every branch code is zero, and the identifier must be a single `0` rather than a string of zeros, and codes are treated as strings to avoid overflow when concatenated. This shows the all-zeros edge case and the overflow-safe string comparison.

What the code will do: a `LargestNumberBuilder` with `buildLargest(List<Integer> codes)` using the a+b versus b+a comparator and the zero guard. The demo builds the largest identifier from a set of branch codes.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the branch codes are `3, 30, 34, 5, 9`.

Step 1: we convert them to strings `3, 30, 34, 5, 9`. Now we sort with the comparator that compares the b-then-a concatenation against the a-then-b concatenation, which puts the piece giving the larger concatenation first.

Step 2: comparing `9` and `5`, the concatenations are `95` and `59`, so `9` comes first. Comparing `5` and `34`, the concatenations are `534` and `345`, so `5` comes before `34`. Comparing `3` and `30`, the concatenations are `330` and `303`, so `3` comes before `30`, which is the counter-intuitive case that numeric sorting would get wrong.

Step 3: comparing `34` and `3`, the concatenations are `343` and `334`, so `34` comes before `3`. Working all pairs out, the sorted order becomes `9, 5, 34, 3, 30`.

Step 4: the first piece is `9`, not `0`, so the all-zeros guard does not trigger. We join the sorted pieces into `9534330`.

Step 5: for the all-zeros demo `0, 0`, sorting leaves `0, 0`, and the first piece is `0`, so the guard returns the single string `0` rather than the invalid `00`. The results are `9534330` and `0`.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T19:50:00Z INFO Largest identifier = 9534330
2026-10-26T19:50:00Z INFO Priority identifier = 9534330
2026-10-26T19:50:00Z INFO All zeros → "0"
2026-10-26T19:50:00Z INFO Zeros case = 0
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [3,30,34,5,9]  → strings ["3","30","34","5","9"]
    │
    ▼
  sort by comparator: (b+a).compareTo(a+b)  (bigger concat first)
    │ "9" vs "5": 95>59 → 9 first
    │ "3" vs "30": 330>303 → 3 before 30
    │ sorted: ["9","5","34","3","30"]
    ▼
  first piece "9" != "0" → join
    ▼
  "9534330"   (all-zeros case → "0")
    ▼
  Output: largest concatenated identifier
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Largest Number problem arranges a list of non-negative integers so their concatenation is the biggest possible number, and the key realization is that sorting numerically is wrong. The piece `3` must come before `30` because `330` beats `303`, even though `3` is numerically smaller. What matters is which arrangement produces the larger concatenated string, not the numeric value of each piece.

So I define a custom comparator on string concatenations. For any two pieces a and b, I compare the string a-then-b against b-then-a and place first whichever yields the larger concatenation. Because both concatenations have identical length, comparing them lexicographically as strings matches comparing them as numbers, which neatly avoids any overflow from building enormous numeric values. I sort all the pieces with this comparator and join them.

The correctness rests on the comparator being a consistent total order, specifically that the a+b versus b+a relation is transitive, which lets a standard sort produce the globally optimal arrangement rather than just locally good swaps. The edge case I always handle is all zeros: joining several zero pieces gives a string like `000`, but the largest number is just `0`, so if the biggest piece after sorting is zero I return the single string `0`.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to assemble numeric branch codes into the single largest concatenated identifier used as a batch priority key, so higher identifiers are processed first, correctly handling cases like a nine beating a thirty. Explaining why numeric sorting fails, the equal-length overflow-safe string comparison, the transitivity that justifies the greedy sort, and the all-zeros guard shows the interviewer that I understand both the trick and why it is provably correct.
